title: Project 2: Lead Generation Workflow
readingMarkdown:
# Project 2: Lead Generation Workflow

Sales teams live on leads: people who might buy. They arrive from forms, webinars, adverts, events, and lists, in every shape and quality. A lead that waits a week for a reply goes cold; a lead sent to the wrong salesperson is wasted; a lead contacted without a lawful basis is a legal risk. A lead generation workflow takes the raw stream and turns it into clean, deduplicated, scored records, routed to the right next step within minutes, with outreach that is personal, accurate, and lawful.

This project builds that workflow. It uses the transformations of Module 7.5, the upserts of Module 7.12, the classification ideas of Module 7.16, and a new subject: the law of marketing email. The lab builds five of the stages that every lead passes through.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A sorting office for people

Picture a busy sorting office for enquiries. Letters arrive in every kind of handwriting: names in capitals, addresses half-filled, the same person writing twice. The first desk copies each onto a clean card. The second desk notices duplicates and staples them together. The third desk weighs each card: is this a serious buyer at a company we serve? The fourth desk decides where it goes: the best to a salesperson, the promising to a series of helpful emails, the rest to the monthly newsletter. And before anything is posted back, a final desk checks that the reply is allowed and contains what the law requires.

```text
   CAPTURE            webinar, form, ad, event, purchased list
      |
      v
   NORMALISE          trim, lower-case emails, tidy names, strip company suffixes, clean phone numbers
      |
      v
   DEDUPLICATE        merge records for the same email; fill gaps from the newer record
      |
      v
   ENRICH             company size, industry, role from enrichment services or an AI research step
      |
      v
   SCORE              fit (who they are) + intent (what they did) -> points -> grade A, B, C
      |
      v
   ROUTE              A -> salesperson (round robin by region)  B -> nurture emails  C -> newsletter
      |
      v
   OUTREACH           AI drafts a personal first email from enrichment facts only
      |
      v
   COMPLIANCE GATE    suppression list, consent and lawful basis, address, opt-out  -> send or hold
      |
      v
   CRM SYNC           upsert by email; log every touch
```

### What the business needs

| Requirement | Decision |
|---|---|
| Speed | A-grade leads reach a salesperson within 5 minutes |
| No duplicates | One CRM record per email address |
| Fair distribution | Leads shared evenly among reps in each region |
| Personal outreach | First emails reference real facts about the lead's company |
| Lawful | No email to anyone suppressed; consent where the law needs it; required content present |
| Measurable | Conversion by source, grade, and rep |

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### Normalisation

Normalisation is Module 7.5's transformation applied to people: one canonical form for each field, so that comparisons work.

| Field | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Email | Trim, lower-case | " Ravi.Kumar@AcmeTools.co.uk " becomes "ravi.kumar@acmetools.co.uk" |
| Domain | Text after the @ | "acmetools.co.uk" |
| Free mail | Domain is a consumer provider | gmail.com, outlook.com |
| Name | Collapse spaces, capitalise words | "ravi  KUMAR" becomes "Ravi Kumar" |
| Company | Strip legal suffixes | "Acme Tools Ltd." becomes "Acme Tools" |
| Phone | International format | "+44 (0)20 7946 0018" becomes "+442079460018" |

The phone example hides a trap. UK numbers are often written with "(0)", the domestic trunk prefix, which must be **dropped** in international format. Stripping all non-digits naively keeps the zero and produces a wrong number. The international standard, ITU-T E.164, writes numbers as a plus sign, a country code, and the national number without its trunk prefix.

### Deduplication

Duplicates arrive constantly: the same person registers for two webinars, fills in a form twice, appears in a bought list. Deduplicating on the normalised email is the reliable baseline, as the upsert of Module 7.12 did. When two records match, they are **merged**: the first record is kept, and empty fields are filled from later ones, so a phone number given on the second form is not lost. Matching on name and company as well catches people who use two addresses, but it risks merging different people, and is better done as a suggestion for a person to confirm than automatically.

### Enrichment

**Enrichment** adds facts the lead did not give: company size, industry, location, the person's role. Data providers sell this through APIs; an AI research step can also read a company's public website and summarise what it does, as the first video shows. Two rules apply. Enrichment facts are claims from a source, so record the source. And an AI research step can be wrong or invent details, so anything it produces that will be shown to the lead, such as "I saw you recently expanded into Leeds", must be checked or grounded in a cited page.

### Scoring

A **lead score** combines two kinds of evidence:

| Kind | Question | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Fit | Is this the kind of customer we serve? | Company size, industry, role seniority, region |
| Intent | Are they showing interest now? | Pricing page visits, demo requests, webinar attendance |

A simple additive model gives points for each signal, caps repeated behaviour so one enthusiast cannot score infinitely, and subtracts for negative signals such as a free-mail address on a business product:

$$\text{score} = \text{size points} + \text{title points} + 10 \cdot \min(\text{pricing visits}, 3) + 30 \cdot [\text{demo request}] - 20 \cdot [\text{free mail}]$$

Thresholds turn the score into grades: 70 or more is A, 40 to 69 is B, below 40 is C. The weights are starting guesses. They should be checked against outcomes: after a few months, compare the conversion rates of each grade, and adjust the weights until A-grade leads really do convert best. A scoring model that is never checked against results is decoration.

### Routing and round robin

Routing applies the grades: A-grade leads go to a salesperson, B to a nurture sequence of helpful emails, C to the newsletter. Free-mail A-grade leads might go to nurture instead, since a personal address on a business product is a weak signal of buying authority.

Assigning A-grade leads fairly is a **round robin**: within each region's team, the next lead goes to the next person in turn. A counter per team, taken modulo the team's size, does it:

$$\text{rep} = \text{team}[\,\text{counter} \bmod |\text{team}|\,]$$

Leads from regions without a team go to a default team. Real systems add capacity, holidays, and specialisms, but the principle is the same.

### AI-personalised outreach

The first email to an A-grade lead is where AI helps most: a short, specific note that shows the sender knows who the lead is. The rule that keeps it honest is **grounding**: the drafting prompt receives only verified facts, the lead's name, company, size, industry, and what they did, and is told to use nothing else. A model told "write a personal email to Ravi at Acme Tools" with no facts will happily invent a recent funding round. Every draft should be reviewed, at least until review data, as in Module 7.16, shows the drafts are reliable.

### The law of marketing email

Marketing email is regulated, and an automation that sends at scale multiplies any mistake. Three regimes appear most often for English-speaking businesses.

**United States, CAN-SPAM.** The Federal Trade Commission's compliance guide states that the law makes no exception for business-to-business email, and sets these requirements: no false or misleading header information; no deceptive subject lines; identify the message as an advertisement; include a valid physical postal address; tell recipients how to opt out; honour opt-out requests within 10 business days, with the opt-out mechanism working for at least 30 days after sending; and monitor anyone sending on your behalf, since responsibility cannot be contracted away. The guide gives penalties of up to USD 53,088 for each separate email in violation, a figure adjusted for inflation from time to time. CAN-SPAM does not require prior consent; it requires honesty and a working opt-out.

**European Union, GDPR.** Processing personal data, including a named person's business email address, needs one of the six lawful bases in Article 6: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests. B2B outreach usually relies on legitimate interests, which requires a documented assessment that the business's interest is not overridden by the person's. Article 21 gives an absolute right to object to direct marketing: once someone objects, their data must no longer be processed for marketing. Electronic marketing rules in each country add further conditions.

**United Kingdom, PECR and UK GDPR.** The Information Commissioner's Office guidance on business-to-business marketing distinguishes **corporate subscribers**, companies and similar bodies, from **individual subscribers**, which include sole traders and some partnerships. Marketing emails to corporate subscribers do not need prior consent under PECR, but must identify the sender and give a valid address for opting out; emails to individual subscribers need consent, or must fall within the narrow "soft opt-in" for existing customers. UK GDPR still applies to the personal data of named contacts at companies.

The compliance gate in the lab checks the mechanical parts of these rules: the suppression list of everyone who opted out or objected, consent for individual subscribers in the UK and EU, a recorded lawful basis for UK and EU contacts, and the presence of a sender identity, a postal address, and an opt-out link. It cannot judge whether a subject line is deceptive, which is why outreach templates need a person's review. This chapter describes the rules for building systems, not legal advice; a business sending marketing at scale should have its process reviewed.

### CRM sync

The final stage writes everything to the CRM with an upsert by email, the pattern of Module 7.12, so retries and duplicates do not create extra records, and logs every touch, each email, call, and status change, against the contact. Suppression must flow both ways: an opt-out recorded in the email tool must reach the CRM, and the CRM's suppression list must be checked before any send.

### Complexity

Normalising and scoring a lead are constant time. Deduplication with a dictionary is linear in the number of leads. Round-robin assignment is constant per lead. The compliance check is constant per message, with a set lookup for suppression.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, normalisation.

```python
import re

FREE_MAIL = {"gmail.com", "yahoo.com", "outlook.com", "hotmail.com", "icloud.com"}
SUFFIX = re.compile(r"[\s,]+(ltd|limited|inc|llc|plc|gmbh)\.?$", re.IGNORECASE)

def normalize(raw):
    email = raw.get("email", "").strip().lower()
    domain = email.split("@")[-1] if "@" in email else ""
    name = " ".join(word.capitalize() for word in raw.get("name", "").split())
    company = SUFFIX.sub("", raw.get("company", "").strip()).strip()
    phone_text = raw.get("phone", "").replace("(0)", "")
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", phone_text)
    phone = ("+" + digits) if phone_text.strip().startswith("+") and digits else digits
    return {"email": email, "domain": domain, "free_mail": domain in FREE_MAIL, "name": name,
            "company": company, "phone": phone, "source": raw.get("source", "")}

print(normalize({"email": " Ravi.Kumar@AcmeTools.co.uk ", "name": "ravi  KUMAR", "company": "Acme Tools Ltd.",
                 "phone": "+44 (0)20 7946 0018", "source": "webinar"}))
print(normalize({"email": "sam@gmail.com", "name": "sam", "company": "Sam's Garden Care"}))
```

- **The email is trimmed and lower-cased, and the domain taken from it.** Every later comparison uses this form.
- **Free-mail domains are flagged.** It is a signal for scoring and routing, not a reason to discard the lead.
- **Names are tidied word by word.** Multiple spaces collapse, and each word is capitalised.
- **Legal suffixes are removed from company names.** "Acme Tools Ltd." and "Acme Tools" then match.
- **The trunk prefix "(0)" is removed before digits are extracted.** The result is "+442079460018", a correct international number, not "+4402079460018".
- **Missing fields become empty strings.** Sam gave no phone, so the phone is empty rather than an error.

Next, merging duplicates.

```python
def dedupe(leads):
    merged, order = {}, []
    for lead in leads:
        key = lead["email"]
        if key not in merged:
            merged[key] = dict(lead)
            order.append(key)
        else:
            for field, value in lead.items():
                if not merged[key].get(field) and value:
                    merged[key][field] = value
    return [merged[key] for key in order], len(leads) - len(order)

LEADS = [normalize(raw) for raw in [
    {"email": "ravi@acme.co.uk", "name": "Ravi", "company": "Acme", "source": "webinar"},
    {"email": "RAVI@acme.co.uk ", "name": "Ravi Kumar", "phone": "020 7946 0018", "source": "form"},
    {"email": "lee@bolt.io", "name": "Lee", "company": "Bolt Inc", "source": "ad"}]]
records, duplicates = dedupe(LEADS)
print(records, duplicates)
```

- **Records are keyed by the normalised email.** "RAVI@acme.co.uk " and "ravi@acme.co.uk" become one person.
- **The first record wins; later records only fill gaps.** Ravi keeps the source "webinar", which is when he first appeared, and gains the phone number from the form.
- **Order is kept.** Records come out in the order each person first appeared.
- **The duplicate count is reported.** A sudden rise in duplicates often means a form is being submitted twice.

Then, scoring.

```python
TITLE_POINTS = [("chief", 25), ("head", 20), ("director", 20), ("manager", 10)]

def score(lead):
    points = 0
    employees = lead.get("employees", 0)
    points += 30 if 50 <= employees <= 1000 else 15 if 10 <= employees < 50 or 1000 < employees <= 5000 else 0
    title = lead.get("title", "").lower()
    points += next((value for word, value in TITLE_POINTS if word in title), 0)
    points += min(lead.get("pricing_visits", 0), 3) * 10
    if lead.get("demo_request"):
        points += 30
    if lead.get("free_mail"):
        points -= 20
    grade = "A" if points >= 70 else "B" if points >= 40 else "C"
    return points, grade

print(score({"employees": 240, "title": "Head of Operations", "pricing_visits": 2, "demo_request": True}))
print(score({"employees": 8, "title": "Owner", "pricing_visits": 1, "free_mail": True}))
print(score({"employees": 30, "title": "Ops Manager", "pricing_visits": 5}))
```

- **Company size gives fit points.** 50 to 1,000 employees is the sweet spot for this business, worth 30; smaller or larger companies get 15; very small or very large get none.
- **The first matching title word gives seniority points.** "Head of Operations" scores 20.
- **Pricing visits score 10 each, capped at 3.** A visitor who refreshed the page twenty times does not outscore a demo request.
- **The head of operations scores 100, grade A.** 30 for size, 20 for title, 20 for two visits, 30 for a demo request.
- **The sole trader on a free-mail address scores minus 10, grade C.** Small company, no seniority match, one visit, and a free-mail penalty.
- **The operations manager scores 55, grade B.** Five visits count as three.

Then, routing with round robin.

```python
REPS = {"uk": ["Amira", "Tom"], "us": ["Jo"], "other": ["Kai"]}

def route(lead, grade, reps, counters):
    if grade == "A" and not lead.get("free_mail"):
        team = lead.get("region") if lead.get("region") in reps else "other"
        turn = counters.get(team, 0)
        counters[team] = turn + 1
        return "sales:" + reps[team][turn % len(reps[team])]
    return "nurture" if grade in ("A", "B") else "newsletter"

counters = {}
print([route({"region": "uk"}, "A", REPS, counters), route({"region": "uk"}, "A", REPS, counters),
       route({"region": "uk"}, "A", REPS, counters), route({"region": "fr"}, "A", REPS, counters),
       route({"region": "uk", "free_mail": True}, "A", REPS, counters), route({}, "B", REPS, counters),
       route({}, "C", REPS, counters)])
```

- **A-grade business leads go to sales, by region.** Three UK leads go to Amira, Tom, and Amira again.
- **Regions without a team use the default team.** The French lead goes to Kai.
- **Counters are kept per team.** Each team rotates independently, and the counters dictionary must be stored between runs, in a table or the tool's data store, or every run would start with the same person.
- **A free-mail A-grade lead goes to nurture.** Strong interest, weak signal of a business buyer.
- **B goes to nurture and C to the newsletter.**

Finally, the compliance gate.

```python
def compliance_issues(lead, message, suppressed):
    issues = []
    if lead["email"] in suppressed:
        issues.append("suppressed")
    if lead.get("region") in ("uk", "eu") and lead.get("subscriber") == "individual" and not lead.get("consent"):
        issues.append("needs_consent")
    if lead.get("region") in ("uk", "eu") and not lead.get("lawful_basis"):
        issues.append("no_lawful_basis")
    if not message.get("postal_address"):
        issues.append("no_postal_address")
    if not message.get("unsubscribe"):
        issues.append("no_opt_out")
    if not message.get("from_name"):
        issues.append("unclear_sender")
    return issues

MESSAGE = {"from_name": "Tidy Tools Sales", "postal_address": "12 Mill Lane, Leeds LS1 4AP",
           "unsubscribe": "https://tidytools.example/unsubscribe?id=abc"}
print(compliance_issues({"email": "ravi@acme.co.uk", "region": "uk", "subscriber": "corporate",
                         "lawful_basis": "legitimate_interests"}, MESSAGE, set()))
print(compliance_issues({"email": "sam@gmail.com", "region": "uk", "subscriber": "individual"},
                        {**MESSAGE, "unsubscribe": ""}, {"sam@gmail.com"}))
```

- **The suppression list is checked first.** Anyone who opted out or objected is never emailed again, whatever their score.
- **Individual subscribers in the UK and EU need consent.** Sole traders and some partnerships count as individuals under PECR.
- **UK and EU contacts need a recorded lawful basis.** Legitimate interests, with its assessment, is the usual one for B2B.
- **Every message needs a postal address, an opt-out, and a clear sender.** These are CAN-SPAM requirements and good practice everywhere.
- **Ravi's email passes.** A corporate subscriber, a recorded basis, and a complete message.
- **Sam's fails four ways.** Suppressed, an individual without consent, no lawful basis, and a message missing its opt-out. Any one issue holds the email.

**Complexity.** `normalize`, `score`, `route`, and `compliance_issues` are constant time per lead. `dedupe` is linear in the leads.

### A lead record after the pipeline

```text
email          ravi.kumar@acmetools.co.uk       (key)
name           Ravi Kumar
company        Acme Tools        employees 240 (enrichment: provider X, 2026-11-16)
phone          +442079460018
sources        webinar 2026-11-10; form 2026-11-14
score          100  grade A      (size 30, title 20, visits 20, demo 30)
owner          Amira             (round robin, uk)
lawful basis   legitimate interests (assessment LIA-2026-04)
subscriber     corporate
suppressed     no
touches        2026-11-16 first email (approved by Amira)
```

### Measuring the pipeline

| Measure | Question |
|---|---|
| Time to first contact for A leads | Are we fast enough? |
| Conversion rate by grade | Does the score mean anything? |
| Conversion rate by source | Which channels are worth paying for? |
| Duplicate rate | Are forms or lists creating noise? |
| Compliance holds by reason | Which part of the process is leaking risk? |
| Opt-out and complaint rate | Is outreach welcome? |

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**Deduplicating on raw emails.** Capitals and spaces create duplicates. Normalise first.

**Merging that overwrites good data.** A later form with an empty company field must not erase the company. Fill gaps only.

**Scores nobody checks.** Weights chosen once and never compared with conversions drift into meaninglessness. Review them quarterly.

**One enthusiastic visitor topping the list.** Uncapped behaviour points reward refreshing a page. Cap them.

**Round robin that resets every run.** Counters held in memory restart at zero, so the first rep gets every first lead. Store them.

**AI outreach with invented facts.** "Congratulations on your funding round" to a company that had none ends the relationship. Ground drafts in verified fields.

**Treating bought lists as permission.** Buying a list does not give a lawful basis or consent. Check each regime's rules before emailing.

**Opt-outs that do not reach every system.** Unsubscribing in the email tool while the CRM keeps sending is a breach and an insult. Sync suppression everywhere.

**Assuming B2B is exempt.** CAN-SPAM covers business email, GDPR covers named business contacts, and PECR treats sole traders as individuals.

**No postal address in templates.** Easy to forget in a plain-text "personal" email, and required under CAN-SPAM.

**Phone numbers with the trunk zero.** "+44 020" fails to dial. Remove "(0)" before formatting.

**Measuring leads, not revenue.** A source that produces many leads and no customers is expensive noise. Track conversion to sales.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** A lead generation workflow captures leads from many sources and passes each through normalisation, deduplication, enrichment, scoring, routing, personalised outreach, a compliance gate, and CRM sync. Normalisation puts fields in canonical form, lower-case trimmed emails, tidy names, companies without legal suffixes, and E.164 phone numbers without the trunk prefix. Deduplication merges records with the same normalised email, keeping the first and filling gaps from later ones. Enrichment adds company facts with their sources, and AI research must be checked before it is quoted to a lead. Scoring adds fit points, such as company size and seniority, and capped intent points, such as pricing visits and demo requests, subtracts for negative signals, and maps scores to grades, with weights checked against real conversions. Routing sends A-grade business leads to salespeople by region in round robin with stored counters, B to nurture, and C to the newsletter. Outreach drafts use only verified facts. The compliance gate checks suppression, consent for UK and EU individual subscribers, a recorded lawful basis, and the presence of a sender identity, postal address, and opt-out, reflecting CAN-SPAM's requirements, which cover B2B email and carry penalties of up to USD 53,088 per email at the time of the FTC's guide, GDPR's lawful bases and absolute right to object to direct marketing, and PECR's distinction between corporate and individual subscribers. CRM sync upserts by email, logs every touch, and keeps suppression consistent across systems.

**Question 1.** Two form submissions arrive: `{"email": "Lee@Bolt.io", "name": "lee", "company": "", "phone": "+44 (0)161 496 0000", "source": "ad"}` and, an hour later, `{"email": "lee@bolt.io ", "name": "Lee Chen", "company": "Bolt Inc", "phone": "", "source": "webinar"}`. Show the normalised records, the merged result, and explain each decision. What would go wrong if the merge let later records overwrite earlier ones?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The first normalises to email "lee@bolt.io", domain "bolt.io", free_mail false, name "Lee", company "", phone "+441614960000" after removing "(0)" and keeping the plus sign, and source "ad". The second normalises to email "lee@bolt.io", domain "bolt.io", free_mail false, name "Lee Chen", company "Bolt", since " Inc" is stripped, phone "", and source "webinar". Both have the same normalised email, so they merge. The first record is kept, so the name stays "Lee", the phone stays "+441614960000", and the source stays "ad", recording where Lee first came from. Empty fields in the first record are filled from the second, so company becomes "Bolt". The name is not upgraded to "Lee Chen", because the first record's name was not empty; a refinement could prefer the longer name, or keep both, but the simple rule only fills gaps. If later records overwrote earlier ones, the merged record would take the second record's empty phone and lose the phone number, and the source would become "webinar", wrongly crediting the webinar with a lead the advert produced, which distorts the measurement of which channels work. Overwriting with empty values is the commonest way merges destroy data.

</details>

**Question 2.** Using the scoring rules in Section 3, score these leads and route them with the UK team of Amira and Tom, starting with fresh counters: (a) 600 employees, "Chief Operating Officer", 1 pricing visit, no demo; (b) 45 employees, "Director of Facilities", 4 pricing visits, demo request, UK; (c) 300 employees, "Head of Procurement", 3 visits, demo request, UK, on a gmail.com address; (d) 2,000 employees, "Engineer", 0 visits, demo request, UK.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

(a) Size 600 is in the 50 to 1,000 band, 30; "chief" gives 25; one visit gives 10; no demo; total 65, grade B, routed to nurture, even though the person is senior, because there is little sign of current interest. Region does not matter for B. (b) Size 45 is in the 10 to 49 band, 15; "director" gives 20; four visits are capped at three, 30; the demo request gives 30; total 95, grade A, a UK business lead, so it goes to sales, and with fresh counters the first UK lead goes to Amira. (c) Size 300 gives 30; "head" gives 20; three visits give 30; demo 30; free mail subtracts 20; total 90, grade A, but on a free-mail address, so it goes to nurture rather than sales, and the UK counter is not advanced. A team might reconsider this rule for strong signals like a demo request, perhaps routing free-mail A leads to a salesperson with a note. (d) Size 2,000 is in the 1,001 to 5,000 band, 15; "Engineer" matches no title word, 0; no visits; demo 30; total 45, grade B, to nurture. Comparing (b) and (d) shows why weights should be checked against outcomes: if demo requests from large companies convert well regardless of title, the model is undervaluing them.

</details>

**Question 3.** A UK company plans to email 5,000 contacts: 3,000 named employees at limited companies, gathered from conference badge scans with a notice explaining follow-up, 1,500 sole traders from a purchased list, and 500 people who unsubscribed last year. Using Section 2, explain which groups can be emailed, what each email must contain, and what the compliance gate in the lab would do.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The 500 people who unsubscribed must not be emailed: their addresses belong on the suppression list, and under GDPR's Article 21 an objection to direct marketing is absolute, while CAN-SPAM, if any are in the US, also requires honouring opt-outs. The gate flags each as "suppressed". The 3,000 employees at limited companies are corporate subscribers under PECR, so marketing email does not need prior consent, but UK GDPR still applies to their personal data, so the company needs a lawful basis, typically legitimate interests supported by a documented assessment; the notice given at the conference helps show the contact was expected. If the basis is recorded, the gate passes them, provided the message is complete. The 1,500 sole traders count as individual subscribers under PECR, so they need consent, or must be existing customers within the soft opt-in, and a purchased list provides neither; the gate flags each as "needs_consent", and also "no_lawful_basis" unless one is recorded, so they should not be emailed. Every email that is sent must identify the sender clearly, give a valid way to opt out that works and is honoured promptly, and in practice include a postal address, which CAN-SPAM requires for any US recipients; the gate checks those fields and holds any message missing them. The gate cannot judge honesty of subject lines or whether the legitimate interests assessment is sound, so the templates and the assessment need a person's review, and a business at this scale should take legal advice.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: Normalise, Deduplicate, Score, Route, and Check Compliance
interactiveLab.context: A company selling workshop tools collects leads from a webinar, a website form, and adverts, and wants each one cleaned, merged, scored, sent to the right place, and contacted lawfully. You will build the five stages of that pipeline: normalising raw leads, merging duplicates, scoring fit and intent, routing by grade with round-robin assignment, and checking each outreach email against consent and anti-spam rules.
interactiveLab.starterCode:
"""
Lab: Normalise, Deduplicate, Score, Route, and Check Compliance
Standard library only. No network calls. Complete the TODO in each step, then press "Run & Verify Step".
"""

steps.title: Normalise a raw lead
steps.instruction: Implement normalize(raw). Treat missing fields as empty text. The email is stripped and lower-cased; the domain is the text after the @, or empty; free_mail says whether the domain is in FREE_MAIL. The name is its words capitalised and joined by single spaces. The company has SUFFIX removed and is stripped. For the phone, remove '(0)', keep only the digits, and put a '+' in front if the stripped text began with '+' and there are digits. The source is kept as given. Normalise Ravi's webinar registration and a sole trader's form. This is normalisation from Section 2. [MOD-7.17]
steps.hintConceptual: Copy every enquiry onto a clean card in the same handwriting: email in lower case, name properly capitalised, company without its legal suffix, and the phone number in the international form a switchboard abroad could dial.
steps.hintSyntax:
email = raw.get("email", "").strip().lower()
domain = email.split("@")[-1] if "@" in email else ""
name = " ".join(word.capitalize() for word in raw.get("name", "").split())
company = SUFFIX.sub("", raw.get("company", "").strip()).strip()
phone_text = raw.get("phone", "").replace("(0)", "")
digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", phone_text)
phone = ("+" + digits) if phone_text.strip().startswith("+") and digits else digits
return {"email": email, "domain": domain, "free_mail": domain in FREE_MAIL, "name": name,
        "company": company, "phone": phone, "source": raw.get("source", "")}
steps.testAssertion:
_r = normalize({"email": " Ravi.Kumar@AcmeTools.co.uk ", "name": "ravi  KUMAR", "company": "Acme Tools Ltd.", "phone": "+44 (0)20 7946 0018", "source": "webinar"})
assert _r == {"email": "ravi.kumar@acmetools.co.uk", "domain": "acmetools.co.uk", "free_mail": False, "name": "Ravi Kumar", "company": "Acme Tools", "phone": "+442079460018", "source": "webinar"}, f"Ravi normalised, got {_r}"
assert normalize({"email": "sam@gmail.com", "name": "sam", "company": "Sam's Garden Care"}) == {"email": "sam@gmail.com", "domain": "gmail.com", "free_mail": True, "name": "Sam", "company": "Sam's Garden Care", "phone": "", "source": ""}, "Free mail flagged; missing fields empty"
assert normalize({"phone": "020 7946 0018"})["phone"] == "02079460018" and normalize({"phone": "+1 (415) 555-0100"})["phone"] == "+14155550100", "Only a leading + keeps the plus; (0) is the trunk prefix, other brackets are not"
assert normalize({"company": "Bolt, Inc"})["company"] == "Bolt" and normalize({"company": "Plc Supplies"})["company"] == "Plc Supplies", "Suffixes are removed only at the end"
assert normalize({"email": "no-at-sign"})["domain"] == "" and normalize({})["free_mail"] is False, "No @ means no domain"
print("Step 1 passed: Ravi Kumar at acmetools.co.uk, phone +442079460018.")

steps.title: Merge duplicate leads
steps.instruction: Implement dedupe(leads). Key each lead by its email. The first lead with a key is copied and kept; for later leads with the same key, fill only the fields that are empty in the kept record with non-empty values from the later one. Return the merged records in order of first appearance and the number of duplicates. Merge Ravi's webinar and form records and a separate lead. This is deduplication from Section 2. [MOD-7.17]
steps.hintConceptual: Staple duplicate cards together, keeping the first card on top and copying onto it only what was missing, never crossing out what was already written.

steps.title: Score fit and intent
steps.instruction: Implement score(lead). Add 30 points for 50 to 1,000 employees, 15 for 10 to 49 or 1,001 to 5,000, otherwise nothing. Add the points of the first word in TITLE_POINTS found in the lower-case title. Add 10 per pricing visit, counting at most 3. Add 30 for a demo request and subtract 20 for free mail. The grade is A for 70 or more, B for 40 or more, otherwise C. Return the points and the grade. Score a head of operations, a sole trader, and an operations manager. This is the scoring model from Section 2. [MOD-7.17]
steps.hintConceptual: Weigh each card on two scales: one for who they are, one for what they have done lately, with a limit on how much any single action can weigh, and a small deduction for signs they are not a business buyer.
steps.hintSyntax:
points = 0
employees = lead.get("employees", 0)
points += 30 if 50 <= employees <= 1000 else 15 if 10 <= employees < 50 or 1000 < employees <= 5000 else 0
title = lead.get("title", "").lower()
points += next((value for word, value in TITLE_POINTS if word in title), 0)
points += min(lead.get("pricing_visits", 0), 3) * 10
if lead.get("demo_request"):
    points += 30
if lead.get("free_mail"):
    points -= 20
grade = "A" if points >= 70 else "B" if points >= 40 else "C"
return points, grade
steps.testAssertion:
assert score({"employees": 240, "title": "Head of Operations", "pricing_visits": 2, "demo_request": True}) == (100, "A"), f"The head of operations, got {score({'employees': 240, 'title': 'Head of Operations', 'pricing_visits': 2, 'demo_request': True})}"
assert score({"employees": 8, "title": "Owner", "pricing_visits": 1, "free_mail": True}) == (-10, "C") and score({"employees": 30, "title": "Ops Manager", "pricing_visits": 5}) == (55, "B"), "The sole trader and the capped visits"
assert [score(x) for x in ({"employees": 600, "title": "Chief Operating Officer", "pricing_visits": 1}, {"employees": 45, "title": "Director of Facilities", "pricing_visits": 4, "demo_request": True},
        {"employees": 300, "title": "Head of Procurement", "pricing_visits": 3, "demo_request": True, "free_mail": True}, {"employees": 2000, "title": "Engineer", "demo_request": True})] == [(65, "B"), (95, "A"), (90, "A"), (45, "B")], "The second recall question"
assert score({}) == (0, "C") and score({"employees": 50})[0] == 30 and score({"employees": 1001})[0] == 15 and score({"employees": 5001})[0] == 0, "Band edges"
assert score({"title": "Chief of Staff and Head of IT"})[0] == 25 and score({"employees": 100, "pricing_visits": 4})[1] == "B", "First matching title word; 60 points is still B"
print("Step 3 passed: 100 for the head of operations, minus 10 for the sole trader, 55 for the manager.")

steps.title: Route with round robin
steps.instruction: Implement route(lead, grade, reps, counters). For grade A without free mail, choose the team named by the lead's region if it is in reps, otherwise 'other'; take that team's counter, default 0; increase the counter; and return 'sales:' followed by the team member at the counter modulo the team size. Otherwise return 'nurture' for grades A and B, and 'newsletter' for C. Route three UK leads, a French lead, a free-mail lead, and B and C leads. This is routing from Section 2. [MOD-7.17]
steps.hintConceptual: Dealing cards around a table, one table per region: each new hot lead goes to the next seat, a lead from a region with no table goes to the spare table, and lukewarm leads go to the post room instead.
steps.hintSyntax:
if grade == "A" and not lead.get("free_mail"):
    team = lead.get("region") if lead.get("region") in reps else "other"
    turn = counters.get(team, 0)
    counters[team] = turn + 1
    return "sales:" + reps[team][turn % len(reps[team])]
return "nurture" if grade in ("A", "B") else "newsletter"
steps.testAssertion:
_counters = {}
_routes = [route({"region": "uk"}, "A", REPS, _counters) for _ in range(3)]
assert _routes == ["sales:Amira", "sales:Tom", "sales:Amira"], f"Round robin in the UK team, got {_routes}"
assert route({"region": "fr"}, "A", REPS, _counters) == "sales:Kai" and route({}, "A", REPS, _counters) == "sales:Kai", "Unknown or missing regions use the default team"
assert _counters == {"uk": 3, "other": 2}, "Counters are kept per team"
assert route({"region": "uk", "free_mail": True}, "A", REPS, _counters) == "nurture" and _counters["uk"] == 3, "Free-mail A leads go to nurture without using a turn"
assert route({"region": "uk"}, "B", REPS, _counters) == "nurture" and route({"region": "uk"}, "C", REPS, _counters) == "newsletter", "B to nurture, C to the newsletter"
assert route({"region": "us"}, "A", REPS, {}) == "sales:Jo" and route({"region": "uk"}, "A", REPS, {"uk": 7}) == "sales:Tom", "Counters can come from storage"
print("Step 4 passed: Amira, Tom, Amira in the UK; Kai for France; nurture for the free-mail lead.")

steps.title: Check outreach against the rules
steps.instruction: Implement compliance_issues(lead, message, suppressed). List, in this order: 'suppressed' if the lead's email is in the suppressed set; 'needs_consent' if the region is uk or eu, the subscriber is 'individual', and there is no consent; 'no_lawful_basis' if the region is uk or eu and no lawful basis is recorded; then 'no_postal_address', 'no_opt_out', and 'unclear_sender' if the message lacks a postal address, an unsubscribe link, or a from name. Return the list. Check a compliant email to a corporate contact and a non-compliant one to a sole trader. This is the compliance gate from Section 2. [MOD-7.17]
steps.hintConceptual: The last desk before the post box: is this person on the do-not-contact list, are we allowed to write to them at all, and does the letter say who we are, where we are, and how to stop hearing from us?
steps.testAssertion:
_msg = {"from_name": "Tidy Tools Sales", "postal_address": "12 Mill Lane, Leeds LS1 4AP", "unsubscribe": "https://tidytools.example/unsubscribe?id=abc"}
assert compliance_issues({"email": "ravi@acme.co.uk", "region": "uk", "subscriber": "corporate", "lawful_basis": "legitimate_interests"}, _msg, set()) == [], "A corporate contact with a basis and a complete message passes"
assert compliance_issues({"email": "sam@gmail.com", "region": "uk", "subscriber": "individual"}, {**_msg, "unsubscribe": ""}, {"sam@gmail.com"}) == ["suppressed", "needs_consent", "no_lawful_basis", "no_opt_out"], "The sole trader fails four ways, in order"
assert compliance_issues({"email": "a@b.com", "region": "us"}, {}, set()) == ["no_postal_address", "no_opt_out", "unclear_sender"], "US contacts need no recorded basis here, but the message content is still required"
assert compliance_issues({"email": "x@y.de", "region": "eu", "subscriber": "individual", "consent": True, "lawful_basis": "consent"}, _msg, set()) == [], "Consent satisfies both checks"
print("Step 5 passed: Ravi's email may go; the sole trader's is held for four reasons.")
